nameStory: This invasive crab earned the name "European Green Crab" because it originally hails from the coasts of Europe and often displays a distinctive green color on its shell. The "green" part can be a bit misleading though - these crabs can actually range from green to reddish-orange depending on their age and when they last molted!
description: The European Green Crab is a medium-sized shore crab that's become an unwelcome visitor to New England's coastlines. These invasive crustaceans have a somewhat flattened, fan-shaped shell that can grow up to about 3.5 inches across. Despite their name, they're not always green - they can appear green, yellow, orange, or even reddish-brown. They're incredibly hardy and adaptable, which has made them successful invaders but problematic for native marine life.

idTips.label: Shell shape and size
idTips.description: Look for a fan-shaped carapace (shell) that's wider than it is long, reaching up to 3.5 inches across - about the size of a large cookie

idTips.label: Five spines on each side
idTips.description: Count exactly five pointed spines along each side edge of the shell behind the eyes - this is the most reliable identifying feature

idTips.label: Variable coloration
idTips.description: Shell color ranges from bright green to yellowish, orange, or reddish-brown, often with darker mottled patterns that feel smooth to the touch

idTips.label: Robust claws
idTips.description: Front claws are noticeably heavy and powerful-looking, with the right claw often slightly larger than the left

idTips.label: Aggressive behavior
idTips.description: These crabs are feisty and will readily raise their claws in a threatening pose when approached - much more aggressive than most native crabs

habitat: European Green Crabs thrive in rocky intertidal zones, muddy estuaries, salt marshes, and shallow coastal waters throughout New England. You'll find them hiding under rocks, in tide pools, and scuttling across mudflats when the tide is out. They prefer areas with some protection from heavy surf but can tolerate a wide range of salinity levels.

seasonality.spring: Crabs become more active as waters warm, emerging from deeper winter refuges. This is prime time to spot them in tide pools and under rocks during low tide.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity season when they're most visible and aggressive. Mating occurs during summer months, and you might see females carrying orange egg masses under their abdomens.
seasonality.fall: Still very active but beginning to move to deeper waters. Great time for observation as they're often foraging heavily before winter.
seasonality.winter: Less visible as they retreat to deeper waters or bury themselves in mud and sand. Can still be found under rocks in protected areas during warmer winter days.

funFact: These crabs are such voracious eaters that they've been caught on camera using tools - picking up rocks and shells to smash open clams and mussels, making them one of the few crabs known to use tools for hunting!
confusionNotes: Most commonly confused with native Rock Crabs, but European Green Crabs have exactly five spines on each side of their shell while Rock Crabs have nine. Memory trick: "Five is the foreign guy" - five spines means it's the invasive European species.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called "European" Green Crabs, they're actually considered one of the world's worst invasive species and have caused significant ecological damage to New England's native shellfish populations. They've been in New England waters since the 1800s but have become much more abundant and problematic in recent decades.
compareHints: Since this is the only green crab species in New England waters, compare it to native Rock Crabs and Jonah Crabs which share similar habitats. European Green Crabs are generally smaller and more aggressive than these natives, with their distinctive five-spine pattern being the dead giveaway. Unlike the chunky, heavy-bodied Rock Crabs, Green Crabs have a more streamlined, athletic build that reflects their active predatory lifestyle.
